strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-explored problem (class-conditional generation under long-tailed training distributions) with a simple, easy-to-implement method that plugs into standard DDPM/DDIM and classifier-free-guidance pipelines.

Empirical evidence is broad and consistent: two backbones (UNet DDPM and DiT/SiT), five datasets (ImageNet-LT 256x256, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT/100-LT), multiple resolutions, and several baselines (CBDM, OCLT, Dispersive Loss, plus balanced-data DDPPM* upper bounds). Improvements over SiT on ImageNet-LT (e.g., FID 33.87 to 25.89 at 40 epochs) and over CBDM/OCLT on TinyImageNet-LT and Places-LT are substantial and consistent across epochs (Table 1), category intervals (Table 3), and sampling budgets (Tables 6-8).

Ablations are informative: the loss-component study (Table 4) and batch-resample study (Table 5) isolate the contribution of L_ucl, L_al, and resampling, and honestly reveal that resampling accounts for a large share of the gain.

Qualitative and latent-space analyses are convincing: same-initial-noise grids (Figs. 4, 6, 7, 9), top-10 nearest-neighbor analysis (Fig. 10), and t-SNE/KDE visualizations (Fig. 8) support the mode-collapse-mitigation claim better than FID alone would.

Good attribution and positioning relative to prior work, including explicit discussion of the concurrent dispersive loss (Wang & He, 2025), UTLO (Khorram et al., 2024), CBDM, and OCLT; the paper is clear about what is inherited and what is adapted (GAN-to-diffusion transfer of conditional-unconditional alignment, timestep weighting t/T).

Reproducibility is mostly well supported: architectures (Fig. 5), training iterations, batch sizes, GPU counts, guidance-strength grid search, and evaluation protocols (10k/50k samples, CFG strength) are documented in the appendix; the limitation on training time (1.6x DDPM, 1.48x SiT, no inference overhead) is stated explicitly.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The unsupervised contrastive loss reduces to a purely repulsive/uniformity regularizer because the anchor latent is used as its own positive (h_pos := h_anc, numerator constant in Eq. 1); this is very close to the concurrent dispersive loss (Wang & He, 2025) the paper itself cites, and the claimed distinction (unconditional vs. conditional latent space, implicit vs. explicit extension) is a modest one. The alignment loss is a fairly direct adaptation of UTLO's conditional-unconditional alignment from GANs to diffusion, with a timestep weighting. The paper is essentially a well-executed combination of two known ingredients.

Some textual claims are overstated relative to the tables. Section 4.2 states 'Our method achieves the best FID score across all three categories on Places-LT and TinyImageNet-LT', but Table 3 shows OCLT's Head FID on TinyImageNet-LT is 20.64, better than CCUA's 21.32. Relatedly, the abstract/contribution claim of not compromising head-class quality is only weakly supported: TinyImageNet-LT Head FID slightly worsens (21.27 to 21.32) versus DDPM.

A large fraction of the reported gain comes from batch resampling, a known trick, rather than from the proposed losses. Table 5 shows resampling alone moves SiT from 33.87 to 28.05 FID, while the full CCUA reaches 25.89; the incremental value of the two new losses is therefore more modest than the headline Table 1 numbers suggest.

The hyperparameters alpha and gamma weighting L_ucl and L_al against L_ddpm (Eq. 7) are not reported in the main text or the visible implementation-details appendix, and no sensitivity analysis for them is given. Since L_al is an unnormalized MSE between two noise predictions whose magnitude varies with the timestep weighting, this omission matters for reproducibility and for judging robustness.

The theoretical justification for the alignment loss is thin. Penalizing the divergence between conditional and unconditional reverse distributions amounts to suppressing the very quantity classifier-free guidance amplifies; the argument that this helps rests entirely on empirical low-frequency-similarity observations (Figs. 3, 11) and on analogy to GAN results (UTLO, Shahbazi et al.). The central claim of 'knowledge sharing from head classes to tail classes' is never directly tested (e.g., no measurement of head-to-tail latent transfer, no experiment isolating tail-class improvement from head-class data).

Comparison breadth at high resolution is limited. On ImageNet-LT 256x256 the only competing methods are the SiT baseline and the concurrent dispersive loss; other long-tailed diffusion approaches (CBDM, OCLT) are evaluated only at 64x64/32x32 with DDPM, so it is unclear whether the large 256x256 gains generalize against a broader set of tail-aware baselines or against longer training schedules (all models are trained from scratch for only 40-160 epochs).

The statistical-significance study (Table 10) uses only three random seeds with near-identical FID values (0.01-0.04 deviation), which is too weak to support the robustness claim; and the unpaired-improvement argument in Appendix A.2 (comparing against DDPPM_bat with large gaps of 1.03/1.8 FID) does not by itself demonstrate that the proposed method closes a meaningful portion of the long-tail gap.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, model-agnostic framework (CCUA) that combines an unsupervised contrastive loss (UCL) with a conditional–unconditional alignment loss (AL), and demonstrates it works on both U-Net-based DDPM and Diffusion Transformer (SiT) pipelines with a clear algorithm box and implementation details.

Empirical evidence is consistent and substantial across five long-tailed datasets: ImageNet-LT (FID 19.95→16.41 at 160 epochs), TinyImageNet-LT (18.67→15.24), Places-LT (13.89→11.99), CIFAR10-LT (5.93→5.56) and CIFAR100-LT (6.95→6.24), outperforming CBDM, OCLT, and the concurrent dispersive loss baseline.

The paper provides good evidence that mode collapse is mitigated rather than just FID improved: tail-class FID (Table 3), head/body/tail category breakdowns, and qualitative visualizations (Figs. 8–10) showing more diverse, less repetitive samples and better coverage of the training distribution.

Ablations are thorough: loss-component analysis (Table 4), batch-resample analysis (Table 5), few-step sampling (Table 8), unconditional generation (Table 9), and a seed-based statistical significance check (Table 10).

The motivation is well articulated, connecting to UTLO for long-tailed GANs and the observation that low-frequency components are shared across classes at early denoising steps (Fig. 3, Fig. 11), and the paper includes an honest limitations statement about increased training time (1.6×) and reproducibility details (GPUs, iterations, CFG strength).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the UCL with self-positive pairs is essentially a uniformity/decorrelation regularizer closely related to the concurrent dispersive loss (Wang & He, 2025) acknowledged by the authors, and the alignment loss is directly adapted from UTLO (Khorram et al., 2024). The core contribution is the combination and adaptation to diffusion rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical derivation of the alignment loss is loose: Eqs. 3–5 claim the KL between conditional and unconditional posteriors 'simplifies to' ||ε_c − ε_unc||², but the derivation drops the time-dependent coefficient β_t/(2α_t(1−ᾱ_t)) arising from the shared variance σ_t²I. The subsequent linear t/T weighting is then applied heuristically, so the stated equivalence is not exact.

Main result tables (Tables 1–3) report single-run numbers without variance/error bars; statistical significance is only examined for CIFAR100-LT with three seeds (Table 10). Given the modest margins on some datasets (e.g., CIFAR10-LT 5.93→5.56), this weakens confidence in the smaller gains.

Baseline coverage is somewhat limited for the long-tail setting: comparisons focus on CBDM, OCLT, and dispersive loss; other long-tail generative strategies (e.g., reweighting/loss-based or augmentation-based methods beyond ADA on CIFAR) are not evaluated, and no code release is indicated.

Some claims are phrased too strongly, e.g., 'above 10% improvement on Recall,' which is a relative figure; the absolute improvement (19.17→23.05) is meaningful but the wording is imprecise. The practical cost of the method (extra forward pass and 1.48–1.6× training time) is only briefly discussed.

strengths: The problem setting (class-conditional diffusion training under long-tailed data) is relevant and practical, and the paper evaluates it broadly: five datasets (ImageNet-LT, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT, CIFAR100-LT), two backbones (U-Net/DDPM and DiT/SiT), multiple resolutions (32/64/256), and multiple samplers (DDIM/ODE, 10/100/1000 steps), with both quality (FID, sFID, KID, IS) and diversity (Precision/Recall, FID_tail) metrics.

The proposed losses are simple to implement, add no inference cost, and the paper provides component ablations (Table 4, Table 5), qualitative comparisons (Figs. 1, 4, 6, 7, 9) and latent-space diagnostics (t-SNE/KDE and top-10 nearest-neighbour analyses in Figs. 8, 10) that plausibly link the dispersion loss to reduced mode collapse for tail classes.

The conditional-unconditional alignment idea is well motivated for diffusion models: the observation that unconditional and conditional trajectories share low-frequency content at large timesteps (Figs. 3, 11) is a reasonable diffusion analogue of the UTLO low-resolution argument, and Table 9 shows the alignment/dispersion losses also improve unconditional generation, a useful consistency check.

The clean (non-resampled) experiments on Places-LT and CIFAR10/100-LT show consistent, if modest, gains over DDPM/CBDM/OCLT (e.g., CIFAR10-LT FID_tail 12.25 -> 10.03, KID 1.64 -> 1.27; Places-LT FID 13.89 -> 11.99, FID_tail 23.74 -> 20.84), and the few-step (DDIM 10) results are competitive.

The paper is generally clearly written, includes an honest note on the training-time overhead (1.6x/1.48x) and an LLM-usage disclosure, and reports an upper bound from balanced-data training (DDPM*_bal), which helps calibrate how much of the gap is recovered.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty relative to closely related work. The Unsupervised Contrastive Loss is a negative-samples-only (uniformity/repulsive) objective, and the authors themselves state that the concurrent Dispersive Loss (Wang & He, 2025) is 'most relevant' and 'similar'; the Alignment Loss is explicitly adapted from UTLO's conditional-unconditional alignment for long-tailed GANs (Khorram et al., 2024), with the delta being (i) applying dispersion to the unconditional latent and (ii) a t/T re-weighting. The related-work section also omits the standard alignment/uniformity analysis of contrastive learning, which is directly pertinent to a loss with no positives.

The headline comparison is confounded. Table 5 shows that batch resampling alone improves SiT from FID 33.87 to 28.05, whereas CCUA without resampling only reaches 32.25; the CCUA row in Table 1 (FID 25.89, Recall 23.05) is exactly the '+Batch Resample' row of Table 5. Thus the main table compares 'proposed loss + resampling trick' against non-resampled baselines (SiT, Dispersive Loss), and the same applies to TinyImageNet-LT (Table 2). A large part of the advertised gain, especially the Recall gain (resampling actually degrades SiT's Recall from 19.17 to 17.26), is therefore not attributable to the proposed losses.

The unsupervised contrastive loss (Eq. 1) is formulated without any embedding normalization, using the anchor itself as the positive. Because the numerator is exp(||h_i||^2/tau) and each negative term is exp(h_i·h_j/tau) with h_i·h_j <= ||h_i||^2, the loss is monotonically reduced by simply scaling the encoder output, i.e., it has a degenerate descent direction and is unbounded below in the scale. The claim that the optimum is 'embeddings uniformly distributed on a hypersphere' does not follow without L2/cosine normalization, which is standard in contrastive learning and is not discussed.

The derivation of the alignment loss does not support the final objective. The KL between the two Gaussian reverse kernels yields a t-dependent coefficient (of order beta_t/(2 alpha_t (1 - alphabar_{t-1}))), which is *larger* for small t, not large t. Eq. (5)'s claim that the KL 'simplifies to' ||eps_cond - eps_unc||^2 is unjustified, and the t/T weighting in Eq. (6) is an independent heuristic that actually contradicts the derived coefficient. The narrative that the loss is 'weighted more for larger timesteps corresponding to the initial stage' is therefore presented as derived when it is not.

Several design choices are ad hoc and unablated: the t/T weight is applied to the contrastive loss only for TinyImageNet-LT/Places-LT but not ImageNet-LT; batch resampling is used only for ImageNet-LT/TinyImageNet-LT with a vaguely specified 're-balanced factor 0.1'; and the loss weights alpha and gamma (Eq. 7) are never given in the main text or appendix, nor is any sensitivity study provided. This is a significant reproducibility gap for a method whose entire contribution is a weighted combination of two auxiliary losses.

Some claims are not supported by the presented evidence. Table 3 shows CCUA is *not* best on the 'Head' super-category of TinyImageNet-LT (CCUA 21.32 vs OCLT 20.64, and marginally worse than DDPM 21.27), contradicting the text's claim of 'the best FID score across all three categories', and the abstract's claim of outperforming 'score-based diffusion model' is not backed by any SBDM baseline in the tables. Table 4 ablates only overall FID without FID_tail/Recall, so the central claim that the tail classes are what improves is not directly evidenced by the ablation.

The 'statistical significance analysis' (Table 10) uses only three seeds and reports FID variation of 0.01-0.04 for their own method, with no comparable variance for baselines or other datasets; it does not establish that the reported differences are significant. Finally, the empirical contribution beyond the concurrent Dispersive Loss is not isolated: since CCUA includes resampling while Dispersive Loss does not, the large gap in Table 1 (25.89 vs 34.00) cannot be read as an advantage of the proposed loss.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: class-imbalanced/long-tailed image generation with diffusion models, where tail-class fidelity and diversity are typically poor.

Proposes a clear and simple framework (CCUA) with two synergistic losses: an unsupervised contrastive loss on unconditional latents to encourage diversity, and a conditional-unconditional alignment loss weighted toward early/large-timestep denoising to share knowledge between head and tail classes.
The method is architecture-agnostic, demonstrated on both U-Net-based DDPM and Diffusion Transformer/SiT backbones, and is easy to implement.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple datasets (ImageNet-LT 256x256, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR-LT) and resolutions, with comparisons to several long-tailed and contrastive baselines including CBDM, OCLT, REPA, Dispersive Loss, and DiffROP.
Strong quantitative improvements are reported, especially on tail-class FID and overall FID/IS, with qualitative visualizations showing reduced mode collapse and greater diversity for tail classes.
Thorough ablation studies cover the two loss components, hyperparameters, latent encoder depth, batch-resampling strategy, and time-scheduler choices, supporting the design decisions.
Good reproducibility details are provided in the appendix, including dataset construction, training configurations, evaluation protocols, and an optimized implementation snippet.

Theoretical motivation via mutual-information decomposition and connection to conditional-unconditional alignment in long-tailed GANs (UTLO) gives useful intuition for why the proposed combination should work.
weaknesses: The main empirical comparisons are potentially confounded by batch resampling: on ImageNet-LT and TinyImageNet-LT, CCUA uses batch resampling while vanilla baselines such as SiT/DDPM do not. The ablation shows that batch resampling alone is a strong baseline, and the gain of CCUA over SiT+BRS is noticeably smaller than over SiT without BRS. Main tables should include the BRS baseline for a fair comparison.

The theoretical claim that directly optimizing conditional InfoNCE leads to a 'trivial solution' of identical latents for same-class images is informal and arguably overstated; a more rigorous analysis would be needed to fully support the argument.

Novelty is moderate: the method combines existing ideas (InfoNCE-style contrastive learning, conditional-unconditional alignment, and knowledge sharing from long-tailed GANs) rather than introducing a fundamentally new principle. The core insight may not be highly surprising to experts in diffusion training.

Some claims are not fully backed by experiments: the abstract and introduction mention outperforming score-based diffusion models (SBDM), but the experiments only include DDPM and SiT; SBDM is not evaluated.

The interaction between the alignment loss and classifier-free guidance is not deeply analyzed. Since CFG relies on conditional-unconditional differences at inference, explicitly aligning them during training could affect controllability, yet this trade-off is not thoroughly explored.
The paper lacks a limitations/broader-impact discussion, and no code release or statistical significance/error bars are provided, which limits assessment of robustness and reproducibility.
Some baselines (e.g., REPA, Dispersive Loss) were not originally designed for long-tailed generation, so their adaptation may not represent their best possible performance in this setting.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly presented method: aligning class-conditional and unconditional generation at large (early) timesteps is grounded in the observed similarity of low-frequency components across classes, which is convincingly validated with visualizations (Fig. 4, Fig. 11).

Simple, general and easy to implement: the two-loss framework applies cleanly to both U-Net-based DDPM and Diffusion Transformer (SiT) architectures with minimal modification, and implementation details (including an optimized parallel forward pass) are provided.

Strong and consistent empirical gains across many datasets (ImageNet-LT 256x256, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10/100-LT), resolutions and architectures, with particularly large improvements on tail-class FID (e.g., FID_tail 52.8 -> 37.0 on ImageNet-LT at 250k).

Thorough evaluation: extensive ablations on hyper-parameters, latent-encoder block choice, time scheduler, and batch-resampling strategy, plus qualitative analysis of mode collapse (Fig. 7, Fig. 10) and reverse-process behavior (Fig. 11).

The mutual-information decomposition (Eq. 2) provides a reasonable, if informal, justification for diversifying unconditional latents rather than conditional latents directly, avoiding the trivial shortcut solution that would collapse all latents of a class to a single vector.
The method demonstrably works without batch resampling (e.g., Places-LT and CIFAR-LT results), showing the contribution is not solely an artifact of the resampling heuristic.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: the two components build heavily on existing ideas (conditional-unconditional alignment from UTL/O [20] for GANs, and InfoNCE / dispersive loss [41] for contrastive regularization). The contribution is mainly the combination and its adaptation to diffusion rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Confounding effect of batch resampling (BRS): on the headline ImageNet-LT results, much of the overall FID gain appears to come from BRS (SiT 33.8 -> +BRS 28.1 -> CCUA+BRS 27.0, Table 12), while CCUA alone yields only modest overall-FID improvements. The main results could more explicitly disentangle BRS from CCUA, though the ablation is provided and the tail-class gains of CCUA on top of BRS are meaningful.

Theoretical analysis is intuitive rather than rigorous; the claim that aligning conditional latents to diversified unconditional latents is 'theoretically ... better than directly diversifying conditional latents' is not formally established.

Training-time overhead is not surfaced in the main comparisons: CCUA is reported as ~1.3x (parallel) to ~1.5x (serial) slower than SiT, with the comparison relegated to a footnote and Appendix A.2. This should be stated alongside the main tables.

The design choice of aligning conditional and unconditional generation at large timesteps could reduce condition influence / controllability; the method is not evaluated on fine-grained or large-vocabulary conditional generation where the class condition matters most, so generalization of the alignment assumption is not fully demonstrated.
The time-adaptive linear weight (t/T) for the alignment loss is justified only empirically on a single dataset (Table 14), and the linear-vs-other scheduler choice is not deeply analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: long-tailed class-conditional image generation, where tail-class fidelity/diversity is genuinely poor.

The proposed CCUA framework is simple and easy to implement, consisting of an InfoNCE-style contrastive loss on unconditional latents plus a conditional–unconditional alignment loss, and it integrates cleanly into both U-Net (DDPM) and transformer (SiT/DiT) pipelines.

The empirical evaluation is broad and reasonably thorough: ImageNet-LT at 256×256, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT/CIFAR100-LT, multiple training budgets (250k–900k), two backbones, and several baselines (CBDM, OCLT, DiffROP, REPA, Dispersive Loss).

Reported gains are substantial, particularly on FID_tail (e.g., 52.8 → 37.0 at 250k on ImageNet-LT), and improvements are accompanied by gains in Recall and Precision, which argues against pure mode-collapse artifacts.

Qualitative evidence (t-SNE embeddings, kernel density estimates, top-10 nearest-neighbor visualizations, low/high-frequency decomposition of the reverse process) supports the claim that CCUA mitigates overfitting to the few tail training images.
Sensible ablations on hyperparameters (α, γ), latent-encoder choice (N/4 vs N/2 vs 3N/4 vs N), and the time-scheduler for the alignment weight are provided.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing is oversold. Equation (2) is a trivial application of the chain rule for mutual information, and the central claim that directly applying InfoNCE to conditional latents 'admits a trivial solution' leading to a shortcut is asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated. No proof, bound, or formal argument is given.

The claimed 'synergy' between the two losses is not convincingly supported by the ablation. In Table 5, the contrastive loss alone (α=0.05, γ=0) achieves FID 27.7, while combining both (α=0.05, γ=0.05) only improves to 27.0 — the alignment loss adds a marginal gain, undermining the paper's central narrative about synergy.

The training-time comparison is not fully fair and is presented in a way that can mislead. CCUA is ~1.3× slower per step (6.7 vs 8.7 steps/s, Table in A.2). Step-based comparisons (250k/450k/700k/900k) therefore confound method with compute. Footnote 5 only addresses one matched pair (700k CCUA vs 900k SiT); the table itself still presents same-step numbers without correction, so the reported deltas overstate the compute-matched advantage.

The 'unsupervised contrastive loss with negative samples only' where the anchor is its own positive is essentially a uniformity-only regularizer and is very close to the concurrent Dispersive Loss [41] the authors acknowledge. The distinctiveness of this component is therefore limited.

Evaluation protocol is ambiguous. The text states Table 1 uses CFG strength 7.5, but Appendix A.1 says a grid search is performed to determine the optimal guidance strength ω for each method. Since the alignment loss directly reshapes the conditional–unconditional difference, tuning CFG per method may partly absorb the effect being attributed to CCUA, and the paper does not analyze this interaction.

The interaction between the training-time alignment loss and inference-time classifier-free guidance is not analyzed, even though both act on the same conditional–unconditional gap. This is a notable omission given that alignment at large t is precisely the regime CFG relies on.

Novelty is incremental: both losses are adaptations of existing components (InfoNCE, UTLO-style conditional–unconditional alignment) to diffusion models, and the claimed differentiators (weighting by t/T, applying contrastive to unconditional rather than conditional latents) are heuristic design choices without principled justification.
No discussion of limitations or broader societal impact (e.g., potential misuse of improved class-conditional generation), which weakens the paper's completeness.

Some claims are unsupported by the presented evidence, e.g., the assertion that the combined loss is 'theoretically and empirically better than directly diversifying conditional latents' — the theoretical part is not established, and the empirical part (Table 5) shows only a small margin.
